# Aggregation and Composition
<!-- Slide 35 -->

## Where Do the Parts Come From? {.smaller}

- Composition stores the part as a member object. Who builds it?

::: notes
Slides 36–47

Topic 2 said composition stores the part as a member object. This topic builds one and finds out when that member is constructed.
:::

<!-- Slide 36 -->

---

## Does This Compile?

::: {style="font-size: 60%;"}
~~~cpp
class Roster {
private:
    int seats;

public:
    explicit Roster(int capacity) { seats = capacity; }
    int size() const { return seats; }
};

class Course {
private:
    string name;
    Roster roster;

public:
    Course(const string& n, int seats) {
        name = n;
        roster = Roster(seats);
    }
};

int main() {
    Course cisp("CISP 400", 30);
    return 0;
}
~~~
:::

::: notes
One file, top to bottom. Roster is the class from 10.01; its only constructor takes an int. Ask students to commit to yes or no before advancing.

Answer: No. g++ reports no matching function for call to 'Roster::Roster()'. The next slide shows why.
:::

<!-- Slide 37 -->

---

## Members Are Built Before the Body

~~~cpp
Course(const string& n, int seats)
    // hidden step 1: build name with string()      fine: string has one
    // hidden step 2: build roster with Roster()    error: there is no Roster()
{
    name = n;                  // assignment, not construction
    roster = Roster(seats);    // too late: roster had to exist already
}
~~~

- g++: `no matching function for call to 'Roster::Roster()'`
- Every member is built before the body runs. If you do not say how, the compiler uses the constructor with no arguments.

::: notes
The comments show what the compiler does that the source code does not say. By the time the body's first line runs, name and roster must already exist. name can be built empty because string has a default constructor, so name = n is just an assignment. roster cannot be built empty, because Roster's only constructor needs an int, so the compiler stops before the body is reached. The fix is to tell the compiler how to build roster before the body: the member initializer list on the next slide.
:::

<!-- Slide 38 -->

---

## Member Initializer List Anatomy

~~~cpp
Course(const string& n, int seats) : name(n), roster(seats) { }
~~~

| Part | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `:` | Starts the member initializer list |
| `name(n)` | Builds `name` from the parameter `n` |
| `roster(seats)` | Builds `roster` by calling `Roster(int)` with `seats` |
| `,` | Separates the members |
| `{ }` | The body runs after every member is built; here it has nothing to do |

::: notes
This is how data reaches the parts: the outer constructor's parameters are passed to each member's constructor. Students saw this syntax in 05.02's examples, such as : name(name), without an explanation. This is the explanation.
:::

<!-- Slide 39 -->

---

## Member Initializer List Anatomy

::: {style="font-size: 60%;"}
~~~cpp
class Roster {
private:
    int seats;

public:
    // The only constructor: a Roster cannot be built without an int
    explicit Roster(int capacity) { seats = capacity; }
    int size() const { return seats; }
};

class Course {
private:
    string name;      // built first: declared first
    Roster roster;    // built second

public:
    // The list builds each member before the body runs:
    //   name(n)        builds name directly from n
    //   roster(seats)  calls Roster(int), so Roster() is never needed
    Course(const string& n, int seats) : name(n), roster(seats) { }

    void print() const {
        cout << name << ": " << roster.size() << " seats" << endl;
    }
};

int main() {
    Course cisp("CISP 400", 30);
    cisp.print();
    return 0;
}
~~~
:::

::: notes
Output: CISP 400: 30 seats

Full program: cpp/course_composition.cpp
:::

## In What Order?

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="60%" style="font-size: 50%;"}
~~~cpp
class Part {
private:
    char id;

public:
    Part(char c) { id = c; cout << "build " << id << endl; }
    ~Part() { cout << "destroy " << id << endl; }
};

class Whole {
private:
    Part first;
    Part second;

public:
    Whole() : second('B'), first('A') { cout << "Whole body" << endl; }
    ~Whole() { cout << "~Whole body" << endl; }
};

int main() {
    Whole w;
    return 0;
}
~~~
:::

::: {.column width="40%"}
. . .

~~~
build A
build B
Whole body
~Whole body
destroy B
destroy A
~~~
:::

::::

::: notes
The list names second first, but members are built in the order they are declared in the class. Destruction runs in reverse, after the destructor body. g++ -Wall warns: 'Whole::second' will be initialized after 'Part Whole::first' [-Wreorder]. Write the list in declaration order.

Full program: cpp/construction_order.cpp
:::

<!-- Slide 41 -->

---

## When the List Is Required

| Member | Why the list is required |
|---|---|
| A class with no default constructor, such as `Roster` | The body is too late to build it |
| `const int limit;` | A `const` cannot be assigned after it is built |
| `Teacher& head;` | A reference must be bound when it is created |
| A base class (11.02) | It is built before the derived part, the same way |

- Everywhere else the list is still preferred: the member is built once instead of built and then assigned.

::: notes

:::

<!-- Slide 42 -->

---

## Copies for Free

~~~cpp
Course cisp("CISP 400", 30);
Course copy = cisp;      // copies name and roster
copy.print();
~~~

Output: `CISP 400: 30 seats`

- `Course` has no copy constructor, copy assignment, or destructor, and it does not need them.

::: notes
This pays off topic 2's Why the Label Matters slide: with member objects, the compiler-generated copy constructor copies each member, and each member's destructor runs automatically. string and Roster already know how to copy themselves. Compare the Rule of Five work an owning pointer would need.
:::

<!-- Slide 43 -->

## Aggregation: Store the Pointer

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="55%" style="font-size: 50%;"}
~~~cpp
// Department does not own its teachers,
// so it has no destructor
class Department {
private:
    string title;
    Teacher* teachers[MAX_TEACHERS];
    int count;

public:
    Department(const string& t) : title(t), count(0) { }

    void addTeacher(Teacher* t) {
        if (count < MAX_TEACHERS) {
            teachers[count] = t;
            count++;
        }
    }

    void print() const {
        cout << title << ":";
        for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) {
            cout << " " << teachers[i]->getName();
        }
        cout << endl;
    }
};
~~~
:::

::: {.column width="45%" style="font-size: 50%;"}
~~~cpp
int main() {
    Teacher lee("Lee");
    Teacher ruiz("Ruiz");

    {
        Department math("Math");
        math.addTeacher(&lee);
        math.addTeacher(&ruiz);
        math.print();
    }                  // math is destroyed here

    cout << lee.getName() << " still exists" << endl;
    return 0;
}
~~~
:::

::::

::: notes
Output: Math: Lee Ruiz, then Lee still exists.

Teacher stores a name and has getName(); see the full program. The teachers are created in main, the department only points at them, and they outlive it.

Full program: cpp/department_aggregation.cpp
:::

<!-- Slide 44 -->

---

## When the Teacher Leaves First

~~~cpp
int main() {
    Department math("Math");
    {
        Teacher lee("Lee");
        math.addTeacher(&lee);
    }                        // lee is destroyed here
    math.print();            // uses a dangling pointer
    return 0;
}
~~~

. . .

- Output: `Math: Lee`. It looks correct, and the program is still wrong.
- `lee` no longer exists. Using it is undefined behavior: garbage, a crash, or output that seems fine.

::: notes
Tested with g++, with and without -O2: both print Math: Lee and exit normally. Compiling with -fsanitize=address reports stack-use-after-scope at the print. Undefined behavior that looks correct is the most dangerous kind, because no test output warns you.

Full program: cpp/dangling_teacher.cpp
:::

<!-- Slide 45 -->

---

## Composition or Aggregation?

| Choose | When |
|---|---|
| Composition, member object | The part lives and dies with the whole and is not shared |
| Composition, owning pointer | The part can be missing or replaced, and the whole still owns it |
| Aggregation, stored pointer | The part lives on its own or is shared |

- An aggregated part must outlive every use the whole makes of it.

::: notes
Prefer the member object; reach for a pointer only when the part can be missing, replaced, or shared. Homework 6, Task 2 asks for an aggregation or composition relationship.
:::

<!-- Slide 46 -->

---

## Summary

- Members are built before the constructor body, so parts with no default constructor, `const` members, and references are built in the member initializer list.
- Composition by member object copies and cleans up for free; aggregation stores a pointer that must never outlive the part it points to.

::: notes

:::
